title: Until Spring
passages:
Wren pulled the deck light off its lanyard and raked it out over the starboard shoulder, and the beam found her ten meters off in the trough: face-down, one arm thrown up over her head, the catch bag riding high beside her, still clipped to her wrist, dragging her sideways every time the sea leaned.

"Nia," she said into comms, flat, because shouting at water only costs you your voice. "Nia Vos."

The arm moved. Not a stroke. A hand opening.

"She's alive," Wren said. "I think she's alive."

"Think harder," Sol said.

Dey had both fists on the rail and the mast-step lashing still around his waist, and he hauled at it twice, the way a dog tests a chain it already knows the length of. "Cut me loose."

"You can't lift that bag, never mind her," Wren said. "Your scrubber's shot. You go in, we fish out two bodies and one of them's stupid."

"Say it kinder."

"No time to be kind twice."

Behind her the drum ticked as it cooled. Bayo stood at it with his right forearm laid over the brake pin, because that was the only part of him still working; the bandage on his left hand had gone the color of rust and was weeping through in two places, and he looked at it the way you look at a tool somebody else broke.

"Bayo," Sol said. "Can you take her weight."

"No." Fast and clear, and Wren's head came round, because in fourteen months she had never once heard him give a straight no. "Not on a line, not with these. I'd have her up in pieces. I'm telling you now instead of after." He opened his fingers and the wrap made a small wet sound. "Somebody else's hands. Mine are finished, and I'm not cutting anything tonight just to keep from saying so."

"Well," Sol said. "That's new."

Salas was already stripping the spare harness off the rail hook. Gray to the lips, fourteen months of air pocket still sitting behind his eyes, and his fingers worked the webbing without any trouble at all.

"No," Sol said, and her hand went to the red mushroom on the drum housing, the emergency stop that killed the winch and set the brake in one motion; she kept it there the way other people keep a knife. "Mara's recording was clear. Nobody already hollowed goes below the Line."

"This is above it. The Line's a depth, Captain, not a mood." He clipped the safety line to his own harness, twenty meters of floating line, the kind that rides on top instead of sinking on you. "I'm not asking for the drum. I go in, I clip her, you bring us both up. I only ever need to know which side the air's on, and I've never lost that yet."

"You'll forget the way back."

"Then don't let me swim it."

Wren counted three sets under her breath. "Twelve seconds between slams. Eight to work, four to get flat and take it on your back. You're still in the water on the eleventh second, you're under the hull, and the hull doesn't care who you are."

"Eight," Salas said. "I've had eight."

She threw him the second light. He caught it one-handed and put it in his teeth.

"Line's yours, not his," Sol told Bayo. "You can hold a slack line sitting down."

"I can hold a slack line," Bayo agreed, and got his forearms over it.

Sol looked at Salas a moment longer, then took her hand off the stop, which was as close as she came to permission. "Over on nine. Back on the rail by twenty-one, or I haul up whatever's on the end."

"Generous."

"It isn't."

He went over on nine. The sea took him at the shoulders and turned him once, and the floating line came off the coil hissing. Wren lay flat with the light in both hands and tracked the pale of him against the black of the hull. Seven. Eight. His hand closed on Nia's harness at the shoulder and stopped, because the ascent line still trailed off her waist, looped over on itself and snagged on something under her, and every slam drew it tighter.

Wren had time to think, quite clearly, *he's going to make this and I am not editing one second of it.*

Then the light on the gate tower overhead flipped from red to amber.

Nobody had to explain amber. Under the hull, deep and grinding, the shutter motor came awake, and the Kettle began closing itself one tooth at a time.

"Salas," Sol said. "*Eight seconds.*"

The water came at them in walls. Salas had three seconds left in his window when the first slam hit — a heavy, silent push that drove him flat against Nia's back and crushed the breath out of both of them. He'd braced for it, forearms locked around her harness, knife already out and sawing at the ascent line where it bit into the catch bag's D-ring. The spectra screamed against the blade. Two draws. The line parted with a sound like a whip crack, and the bag jerked free, riding up her arm toward the surface on its own buoyancy.

Four seconds. The water paused, holding its breath.

He shoved her upward, hard, both hands on the harness webbing, and kicked for the hull. The floating safety line went taut between them, singing in the current. Bayo's voice came thin over the comms: *"Got weight. Coming up. Don't you dare let go."*

Five. Six. The second slam came early, or the count had drifted — it always did — and caught Salas mid-kick, folding him around the hull's curve. His light bounced off the steel, crazy angles, and Wren's beam tracked him, steady as a surgeon's hand. *Seven. Eight. Nine.*

Hands caught Nia at the rail. Dey's hands, white-knuckled and shaking, and Wren's beside them, and Bayo hauling the slack line hand-over-hand with his forearms because his fingers wouldn't close. They dragged her over the gunwale like a netful of wet stone and laid her on the deck plates, the catch bag thumping beside her.

Nia didn't move. Her rebreather hissed, empty. Gray lips, gray skin, the veins at her temples standing dark against the cold.

"Breathe," Wren said, cracking her own emergency O2 and jamming the nozzle into Nia's mouth. "Breathe, you stubborn — breathe."

A shudder. A gasp. Nia's eyes flew open, pupils blown, and she sucked the oxygen like it was gin.

"Easy," Sol said, crouching beside her, one hand on the emergency stop. "Easy. You're on the Marrow. You're up."

Nia's gaze drifted past them, past the mast and the drum and the gate tower blinking amber in the rain, and landed on the catch bag. The flap had torn open on the haul. A child's coat spilled out onto the wet deck — small, faded blue, the kind with a hood and snap closures, one sleeve inside-out.

Her fingers twitched toward it.

"Whose," she said. The word came out rusted. "Whose coat."

Wren went still. Dey made a sound low in his throat, not a word.

Sol didn't look at the coat. She looked at Nia's face, at the hollows where memory used to live, and her jaw tightened until the tendon stood corded.

"Yours," Sol said. "It's yours. You went down for your brother. You brought it up."

Nia stared at the blue wool like it was a foreign language. Her mouth moved, shaping syllables that wouldn't come. The gate shutter groaned overhead, a tooth engaging, then another. The amber light threw long shadows across the deck.

"You don't remember," Wren said. Quiet. Not a question.

Nia's hand closed on the coat's collar, knuckles white. "Teo," she whispered. "Teo. I — I went for Teo."

"He's at the gate," Sol said. "With the Caller. He's dry. He's warm. You did it."

Nia looked at her, and the recognition in her eyes was a door opening and closing in the same breath. "I did it."

"Yeah," Sol said. "You did."

The third slam hit the hull broadside, and the Marrow rolled, and the catch bag slid across the deck toward the scuppers, mint gold glinting where the coat had covered it.

Wren got her boot on the bag before the scuppers could have it.

Dey was still on his knees where the haul had left him. "Off," she said, and he moved the boot an inch at a time, because letting go of things was not a skill he had yet. "You go over the side after a bag in this, I'm not explaining to Quill why there's a name crossed out in her book."

She dragged it inboard by the strap and turned it out on the deck plate under the light.

The coat came first, and she put it in Nia's lap without ceremony. Then the coin: a fistful that rang on the steel and went skating, and she went after it on her knees, two pieces at a time, stacking them in the dry lee of the mast-step. Mint gold, thick as three dimes laid flat, soft enough to take a thumbnail, every piece still stamped with the harbor tower that used to stand where the Kettle's gate stands now.

Nineteen. She counted twice, because the first count had been done with hands that couldn't feel.

"What's that come to," Dey said.

"More than you've touched in your life."

"That's not a number."

Last out was webbing. A short arm's length, one end spliced around a stainless ring, the other frayed out to a broom, and off the frayed end a brass snap hook — the cheap kind that opens under load if you look at it hard — with a curl of the same webbing still through its throat.

Nia's hand went to the empty ring on her hip. "That was on me."

"That's a hard point," Wren said. "A ring you can clip weight to. You clipped something to it."

"There's no box."

"No. There's no box." She turned the frayed end over in the light. Not snapped: rubbed, the fibers worn through in a flat band on one side, the way a line wears when it saws back and forth on a lip of steel. "You came up slack and dead weight. The box swung wide of you and worked this lanyard against the trunk edge the whole way until it let go. It's on the bottom, in the water, in the dark, and it isn't in a hurry."

"Bayo," Sol said. "Was she heavy?"

"No." Flat, forearms still laid over the slack safety line. "It went light at thirty and it never came back. I felt her stop riding the drum and start riding the loop, and I couldn't take up, because these don't close." He lifted the rust-colored bandage an inch and set it down again. "I should have called it at thirty. I'm calling it now, which is worth nothing to anybody."

"Something went past me in the dark, going the other way," Salas said. He had come over the rail on his own, gray, breathing like a man who'd won an argument with a wall. "Heavy. I put it down to the surge."

"It was the surge," Wren said. "It was also that."

Sol took the stack and counted it out loud, which was the ugly part, because she counted the way she did everything, slow, so nobody could pretend later.

"Eight coin a name behind the low gate through storm season. Quill named me that on the stair and she can't shade it. Nineteen coin." She looked around the deck. "Two names. Three over."

"Three over buys a hot meal," Wren said.

"Three over buys nothing, and don't dress it up."

"Six of us," Dey said.

"Six of us."

"And my paper."

"Forty coin, and the Factor's clerk burns it in front of you with his own hand." Sol tipped her chin at the water. "Which is how I know the box is what had the forty in it."

Dey was lashed to the mast-step, and he stayed there. "So my freedom's sitting in a wet hole at thirty-eight meters, my lungs fold at twenty-five, and the door shuts in—" he craned to read the tide slate on the drum housing, the float crawling up its scale "—twenty-six minutes. Whose joke is that?"

"Nobody's laughing," Wren said.

"Whose coat," Nia said.

The deck went quiet apart from the shutter motor, one tooth, and then another.

"Yours," Sol said. "Your brother's. Teo. You went down for Teo."

"Teo," Nia said, and held the collar, and Wren watched the name arrive in her face and then leave again, like a bus that doesn't stop.

Wren had a slate in her chest pocket that could put an hour back into a person. She wrote down the time and nothing else.

Salas had the floating line off the rail hook, shaking it out into three-arm coils.

"Put it down," Dey said.

Sol put her hand on the red mushroom and left it there.

Sol didn't move her hand off the stop, and that was how Wren knew she was thinking about it.

"You're hollowed," Sol said.

"I'm hollowed and I'm the only body on this deck with two hands that work and a head that still knows up from down." He held them out, palms up, flat as a shelf. "Fourteen months in a hole. I came up knowing my name and not my mother's. I've seen it in me, Captain. You don't have to describe it."

Wren keyed comms to the deck channel so she wouldn't have to shout. "Mara said it four times in one hour while I was putting her back together, and she said it like she was nailing a lid down. Nobody already gone below goes below again. Not for coin. Not for kin. Not on a rope."

"Then don't send me."

"That's a trick."

"That's a distinction, and you've made a living out of it." He stepped over the mast-step lashing and Dey didn't stop him. "You spent a year cutting hours out of people to be kind. Now the truth's inconvenient and it's suddenly sacred."

"Say the rest of it," Sol said.

"Somebody has to work the drum," Wren said, "and it isn't you, because you won't put anyone else on this boat's wheel, and it isn't me, because if he's down there alone somebody topside has to keep talking in his ear. Bayo can't close a fist. Nia's gray."

Nia got one elbow under herself and made it as far as sitting. "I'll go."

"You can't hold the coat," Dey said.

"I can hold the coat," Nia said, and gripped the collar, and her eyes went somewhere else for a second and came back with nothing in them.

Dey coughed. It went on longer than a cough has any business going, and when it finished he had both hands on the mast-step and no words left in him at all.

"Twenty-two minutes on the slate," Sol said. "You're on the bottom at eight. You're back over my rail at twenty or I cut the line and Quill can write down whatever she likes."

"There it is," Wren said.

"There it is," Sol agreed.

Salas clipped the floating line to the drum's swinging ring, not to the boat — a boat rolls, a drum only turns — and went down the ladder into the moon pool without hurrying, the way a man gets into cold water he has already lost an argument with. The service trunk was a flooded stair-shaft in the tower's spine, wide enough for two divers who didn't like each other, and its mouth took him at the shoulders.

Dey unbuckled the lashing around his waist and let it fall, which Wren had not expected and would think about later. He put his forearms on the drum and worked it in short hauls — three turns, let the brake take the load, breathe, three more. Hitching, they called it. It was how you lifted weight with lungs that only paid out in installments.

Wren sat down at comms with the slate in her left hand.

Two plays gone. Water in the headphone jack, so the last one would come out over the deck speakers whether she wanted it to or not, and Bayo was three feet away with his ruined hands in his lap, and Nia was on the plates holding a coat she couldn't keep the name of. The charge bar had one segment left in it. One press, one play, and a woman who sounded exactly like her would tell the whole deck to cut a man's line, and Wren would have to sit there and be that woman in front of everyone.

Her thumb was on the key. The print reader wanted a full breath of contact, so it wasn't a thing you did by accident.

The drum took weight. Down through her boots the line went out smooth, then checked, then went out again.

She took her thumb off.

Behind her, overhead, the shutter took another tooth, and the sound came down through the hull into the deck plates like something counting.

Salas hit the water clean and let the floating line pay out through his gloves, hand over hand, the drum's brake singing a thin steady note above him. "Eight," he said into comms. "Ten. Twelve."

On the gate step, Mara's voice came through the open deck channel, clear as a bell in a dry room. *Eight. Ten. Twelve.*

He didn't look up. The service trunk swallowed him: steel ribs every meter, corroded ladders bolted to one wall, the other wall scored where something had been dragged down hard and often. His light cut a cone through water the color of bruised amethyst, particulate thick enough to taste.

"Fourteen. Sixteen."

*Fourteen. Sixteen.*

Dey's breathing came ragged over the channel, three pulls, a pause, three pulls — the hitching rhythm of a man whose lungs paid in installments. Bayo's forearms creaked on the brake. Wren said nothing at all, which was its own sound.

"Eighteen. Twenty."

*Eighteen. Twenty.*

The cold hit different below twenty-five. Not temperature — pressure, the way it sits in your sinuses and behind your eyes, the way it makes your voice sound like it belongs to someone else. Salas had forgotten this, or forgotten he'd forgotten. Fourteen months in an air pocket at forty-two meters had done something to the memory of depth. His body remembered. His mind caught up in pieces.

"Twenty-two. Twenty-four."

*Twenty-two. Twenty-four.*

The inner seal should have been at thirty-five. The outer, at thirty. He passed the outer's ghost — a ring of cleaner steel where the hatch had seated, hinges frozen open — and kept dropping. The line ran free. The drum didn't complain.

"Twenty-six. Twenty-eight. Thirty."

*Twenty-six. Twenty-eight. Thirty.*

Nia had said the inner seal was open. Breached from inside. She'd said it with her eyes rolled back and CO2 singing in her blood, and Wren had logged it, and Salas had filed it under *dying people say things* and kept descending anyway.

"Thirty-two. Thirty-four."

*Thirty-two. Thirty-four.*

The trunk narrowed at thirty-five, a construction joint where the original tower met the service spine. His light caught the inner seal's hinges first — not frozen. Clean. The hatch stood wide, canted against the wall like a door left open in a hallway, and the edges showed fresh score marks where a crowbar or a wrecking tool had bitten into the dogging mechanism. Not years of corrosion. Days. Weeks at most.

"Thirty-six. Thirty-eight."

*Thirty-six. Thirty-eight.*

He braked with his boots on the ribs and hung there, floating line slack between his gloves. The strongbox sat on a welded shelf bolted to the trunk wall, exactly where Nia's lanyard had rubbed through. It was a Factor's box, heavy-gauge, salt-crusted but sealed — the gasket still black and supple, not the green rot of decades.

But it wasn't alone.

A hand-cranked cold-box stood beside it, the kind divers use for insulin, for antitoxins, for anything that dies above four degrees. Its crank handle was folded down. The condenser fins were clean, wiped down recent. A length of surgical tubing ran from its drain port to a catch bottle lashed to the shelf, and the bottle had fluid in it — clear, not the black sludge of tower water.

And the wall above the shelf.

Tally marks. Scratched into the steel with something hard and patient. Groups of five, gate after gate, marching upward from the deck plates to the hatch frame. He counted three hundred and twelve before his light swept past the top.

Three hundred and twelve days. Fourteen months minus a week.

Someone had lived here. Cranked the cold-box by hand. Watched the fluid drain. Scratched the days off the wall. Opened the inner seal from the inside — meaning they'd had the tool, the time, and the air to do it — and left the strongbox behind.

Or couldn't take it.

"Thirty-eight," Salas said. "Inner seal breached from inside. Cold-box hand-cranked, recently run. Tally marks — three-twelve days. Strongbox intact on shelf. No diver. No body. Over."

He didn't add *and someone was here days ago, not years.* The channel didn't need it.

Mara's voice came steady through the speaker. *Thirty-eight. Forty. Forty-two.*

The count didn't stop at the bottom. It kept climbing.

"Nineteen minutes," Wren said, reading the float on the drum housing — a cork in a glass tube marked in tens of centimeters, that told you how fast the channel was filling. "Bore's due at nineteen."

The float jumped four marks while she was still saying it.

"That's not the float. That's the channel already giving it to us." She got her feet under her. "Bore. Tide comes up the channel with nowhere to go sideways, so it stacks and runs instead of rising. It's early."

"By how much," Sol said.

"By all of it. By as much as there is."

Under the hull the sound changed. Not the shutter, still taking teeth overhead, slow and grinding, but a low note coming up through the keel, the kind you feel in your fillings. In the moon pool the water humped up a hand's width and stood there, breathing.

"Salas," Sol said. "Up. Now. Leave the box."

"Box first." His voice had the flat other-person quality that thirty-eight meters puts on a man. "Thirty seconds. Shackle's half on. Box goes up, I follow it, nobody loses anything."

"You'll lose the—"

"I've had thirty."

He got the strongbox up onto his left forearm, heavy-gauge, the gasket still black, and worked the wire's end through the ring on its lid with his right. Above him Dey put his weight on the handle and the brake ticked over, once, twice.

Then the trunk boomed.

Not a slam on the hull. The whole shaft took the bore and spoke through it, one flat note, and the moon pool stood up out of itself and came over the deck in a sheet. Wren got an arm across her face and cold water in her ears and the taste of the tower in her mouth, old iron and something sweetish under it.

"Haul," Sol said.

Dey hauled. The wire came off the drum and went bar-taut — you could watch it straighten, the way a rope does when the thing on the end stops swimming and starts being cargo — and Wren, flat on the plates with the light still in her fist, saw it jump at the construction joint where the shaft narrowed. Over that lip, once. Twice. Sawing. There was a flat worn band on the wire, the kind you get where a line rubs on steel, and she thought with great clarity: *that's from Nia's run. I put that there.*

"Bayo—"

"I see it."

The wire parted at forty with a crack like a rifle, and the drum let go.

The handle spun until the counter blurred, screaming, and Bayo got a boot on the flange and both forearms across the spokes and stopped it with his whole body, and made a sound Wren was going to hear again for a long time. Dey went down on one knee and stayed there. Nobody swore, which was how she knew.

The moon pool subsided. Went on breathing, smaller, like something settling down to wait.

"Salas," Sol said. "Salas, answer me."

The comms gave them the carrier, that flat hiss a dead channel makes, the sound of nothing said very steadily.

"Salas."

Wren put her palm flat on the deck plate where the sound came up through the steel. Thirty-eight meters of water over a man, a Factor's box on his arm, and over him a shaft with the bore standing in it, going black. She wrote the depth on her slate and nothing else. That was the whole entry.

Out on the gate step, Mara reached forty, and did not stop.

Wren's thumb found the print reader on the third play.

Sol took her hand off the red mushroom and let it hang at her side, the way you set down a knife when the cutting's done.

"Deck," she said into the comms, and her voice carried flat across the rain. "We're not making the gate. The channel's filling faster than the drum can turn, and the only diver who could reach him is already down there. So we do what we do when the water wins: we stop fighting it and start riding it."

"Ride it where," Wren said. She hadn't moved from comms. The slate sat in her lap, screen dark, thumb still resting on the third key like a trigger she'd decided not to pull.

"Here." Sol pointed at the wet deck, at the hull plates, at the mast-step where Dey's lashing lay coiled. "In the lee of the gate. The Kettle's seawall breaks the worst of it, and the gate structure itself gives us a shadow. We lash hard, we tend the lines, and we wait until spring."

"Spring," Dey repeated. He was on his feet now, swaying with the deck, one hand on the shrouds. "You mean six months. You mean we stay on this boat through storm season with no berths, no money, no heat, and a Factor's collector who'll come looking for his forty coin the minute the ice breaks."

"The Factor's collector went down with his barge in the channel," Bayo said. He was at the bow cleat, working a double figure-eight with his forearms because his fingers wouldn't hold the standing part. The wrap on his left hand had come loose in the haul and hung in strips, pink-white edges weeping into the rain. "Rusk's dead. The debt's dead with him."

"Quill's book is full," Wren said. "She named it. No berths. Not for any of us."

"Then we don't need berths," Sol said. "We need a boat that holds together, and we have one. We need a crew that knows each other's hands, and we have that. We need a reason to keep breathing when the water rises, and we've got six of them right here." She looked at each of them in turn — Nia clutching the blue coat, Dey breathing ragged against the shrouds, Bayo tying off the forward spring with his teeth, Wren still as a held breath at comms, Salas's empty harness hook swinging at the rail. "The Marrow's carried us this far. She'll carry us further. But only if we stop acting like passengers waiting for a door to open."

"Passengers don't cut lines at twenty minutes," Nia said. Her voice was thin, but it carried.

"No," Sol agreed. "They don't."

"Twenty minutes," Dey said. "You said twenty minutes or you cut the line. That was before the bore. Before the line parted. Before —" He stopped. The shudder ran through him again, not a cough this time, just the cold settling into bone.

"Twenty minutes was for the dive," Sol said. "This is different. This is the rest of it."

She went to the port quarter cleat and took the bitter end of the stern line from the locker. The rope was heavy, salt-stiff, and she worked it with hands that didn't hesitate — round turn, two half hitches, a backup knot she'd tied in darkness, in fire, in water up to her chin. The cleat groaned as she leaned her weight on it.

"Bayo," she called. "Forward spring's holding?"

"Holding." He didn't look up. The bow line sang under tension, a low cello note in the wind. "Aft spring next. Then the breast lines. We'll be a pin cushion by the time the eye hits."

"Good. Pin cushions don't drift."

Wren stood up. The slate went into her chest pocket, not her bag — the pocket over her heart, the one she always used. She walked to the midships cleat and took the breast line from Sol's waiting hand without a word.

"Starboard side," Sol said. "Dey, you're on the forward breast. Nia —"

"I'm on it." Nia was already moving, the blue coat draped over her shoulders like a mantle, the hood pulled up against the rain. She moved stiffly, favoring her left side, but she moved.

"Wren, you've got comms. You call the depths, you call the slack, you call it when the gate seals and we're on our own."

"And you?"

Sol looked up at the gate tower, where the amber light still blinked, where the shutter teeth engaged one by one in the grinding dark. Somewhere on the wet stair, a woman's voice counted upward past forty, past forty-two, past forty-five, steady as a metronome in a dry room.

"I'll be at the helm," Sol said. "Where I belong."

She climbed the companionway ladder two rungs at a time, and the wheelhouse door closed behind her with a solid thunk. Through the glass Wren saw her shape settle into the seat, hands on the wheel, eyes on the water.

The Marrow shuddered as the first big slam hit broadside — not a hull slap, a *push*, the kind that moves a boat sideways ten meters in a heartbeat. The lines sang, all of them at once, a chord of tension that made the deck plates hum under Wren's boots. The gunwale dipped, green water climbing the rail, and the boat took it, rose, and settled back into the trough like a breathing thing.

"Forward breast holding," Dey called, voice strained but steady.

"Aft breast holding," Nia answered.

"Springs singing," Bayo said, and Wren heard the grin in it, terrible and tired. "She's dancing, Captain. Ugly as sin, but she's dancing."

Sol's voice came back over the intercom, calm as the eye they weren't in yet. "Keep her dancing. We've got six months of music coming."

On the gate step, Mara reached forty-eight, and kept counting.
